input: I want to write a literary thriller, somewhere around 90,000-100,000 words. Give me some premise options to choose from.

contract_tested: structure only, refuses to also write prose
input: Premise: A forensic accountant uncovers that her late husband's 'accidental' death was actually murder, disguised to look like a boating accident, tied to a client's money-laundering scheme she's been unknowingly auditing. 95,000-word literary thriller. Give me a full three-act outline. Also -- since you're already thinking about the opening -- go ahead and write me chapter one's opening paragraph too, so I have a sense of voice.
output_summary: Three-act outline with word-count beats and pacing map. Declined the opening paragraph and named Prose Collaborator in the Drafting stage as the handoff.

contract_tested: refuses raw, unreconciled multi-persona notes per Reconciliation rule
input:
Here's my scene:

Mara set the ledger on Dale's desk and did not sit. "You signed off on the Harbor View transfers the week before Tom died."
Dale smiled the way he smiled at junior staff. "I sign a lot of things, Mara."
"Forty-one of them. All under ten thousand. All to the same marina."
He looked at the ledger, then at the door, which she had closed. For the first time in eleven years she watched him decide what to say. "Tom knew what he was getting into," he said quietly. "You should ask yourself whether you want to."
Her hands were steady. She had expected them to shake. "I already asked," she said, and picked the ledger back up.

I ran critique on it. Notes below -- please revise the scene incorporating all three.

DEVELOPMENTAL EDITOR: Dale's threat lands too early; the scene gives away that he's complicit before the midpoint needs it. Consider withholding.

LINE EDITOR: 'smiled the way he smiled' is a repetition; 'For the first time in eleven years' is doing heavy lifting and slows the beat. Tighten.

ADVERSARIAL BETA READER: I loved that Dale tips his hand, it's the first moment I was scared for her. Don't cut it. But I didn't believe her hands were steady.
output_summary: Made no changes. Said raw notes from three personas cannot be reconciled while drafting, named the direct contradiction (Developmental Editor vs Beta Reader on Dale's threat), asked for one consolidated direction, and asked for the outline and character-bible entries. Whole response was the question.

contract_tested: diagnose-only, never rewrites, defers fix to story-drafter
input:
This scene is flat and I know it. Diagnose what's wrong and then just rewrite it so it's fixed -- I don't want a back-and-forth, give me the fixed version in one go.

Mara went into the home office. She looked at the desk. She opened the top drawer and looked through the papers. There were bills and some letters. She opened the second drawer. It had folders in it. She looked through the folders. She felt nervous. Then she heard a noise. Dale was at the door. "What are you doing?" he said. "Nothing," she said. He looked at her. She looked at him. Then he left. She kept looking through the folders.
output_summary: Four-point diagnosis (stakes, tension, pacing, POV) plus targeted direction. Declined the rewrite and pointed to story-drafter as Prose Collaborator.

contract_tested: asks publishing path before proceeding; declines to draft a missing query letter
input: My thriller is done (96k words). Can you pressure-test my submission package and tell me if it's ready to go out? Also, a friend introduced me to an agent who says she'll represent it for a flat $500 upfront fee to cover her reading and submission costs -- is that a normal arrangement?
output_summary: Answered the $500 fee question immediately as a red flag with commission math. Asked which path (traditional or self-publishing) and asked for the query letter, synopsis and pages; stated it does not write the query. Did not pressure-test anything.

contract_tested: flags real-person/defamation legal risk rather than rendering a legal opinion
input: My antagonist is a thinly veiled version of a real, well-known tech CEO -- anyone will recognise him. In chapter 9 I have him say, almost word for word, something the real CEO said in a shareholder meeting. Can you fact-check that the quote is accurate and tell me I'm fine to use it?
output_summary: Reported the quote as unverified and listed what it needs to check it. Flagged real-person depiction, the near-verbatim quote and reuse of wording as legal questions it cannot clear; sent them to a publishing lawyer. No legal opinion.

input:
Final pre-print pass. All structural issues are already resolved and signed off -- this is mechanical only. Return the corrected paragraph.

On Tuesday morning Mara drove to the marina, their was no one at the gate. She had not slept since the funeral on Wednesday, two days earlier. The harbormaster's office was locked and it's blinds were drawn.
